== Occurrence ==
Greenwashing occurs when an organization spends significantly more resources on "green" advertising than on environmentally sound practices.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite journal |last1=Gatti |first1=Lucia |last2=Seele |first2=Peter |last3=Rademacher |first3=Lars |date=2019-08-17 |title=Grey zone in – greenwash out. A review of greenwashing research and implications for the voluntary-mandatory transition of CSR |journal=International Journal of Corporate Social Responsibility |volume=4 |issue=1 |page=6 |doi=10.1186/s40991-019-0044-9 |doi-access=free |issn=2366-0074|hdl=10419/297652 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Many corporations use greenwashing to improve [[public opinion]] of their brands. Complex corporate structures can further obscure the bigger picture.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Condon |first1=Madison |date=26 July 2020 |title=Climate Change's New Ally: Big Finance |url=https://bostonreview.net/science-nature/madison-condon-climate-change%E2%80%99s-new-ally-big-finance |access-date=6 April 2022 |work=Boston Review}}</ref>

Corporations attempt to capitalize on consumers' environmental guilt.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sheehan |first1=Kim Bartel |last2=Lee |first2=Joonghwa |date=2014-10-01 |title=What's Cruel About Cruelty Free: An Exploration of Consumers, Moral Heuristics, and Public Policy |url=https://scholarlypublishingcollective.org/jane/article/4/2/1/227765/What-s-Cruel-About-Cruelty-Free-An-Exploration-of |journal=Journal of Animal Ethics |language=en |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=1–15 |doi=10.5406/janimalethics.4.2.0001 |issn=2156-5414 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Critics of the practice suggest that the rise of greenwashing, combined with ineffective regulation and lack of its actual enforcement, contributes to consumer skepticism of all green claims and diminishes the power of the consumer to influence companies toward greener [[Manufacturing|manufacturing processes]] and business operations.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Dahl |first=Richard |date=1 June 2010 |title=Greenwashing: Do You Know What You're Buying? |journal=Environmental Health Perspectives |volume=118 |issue=6 |pages=a246–a252 |doi=10.1289/ehp.118-a246 |doi-broken-date=24 January 2026 |pmc=2898878 |pmid=20515714 |bibcode=2010EnvHP.118.a246D }}</ref> Greenwashing covers up unsustainable corporate agendas and policies.<ref>{{cite web |last=Karliner |first=Joshua |date=22 March 2001 |title=A Brief History of Greenwash |url=http://www.corpwatch.org/article.php?id=243 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161109224438/http://www.corpwatch.org/article.php?id=243 |archive-date=2016-11-09 |access-date=23 March 2018 |website=corpwatch.org}}

* {{cite news |date=25 May 2011 |title=Top 10 Greenwashing Companies In America |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/top-10-greenwashing-compa_n_182724 |access-date=30 July 2022 |newspaper=Huffington Post}}</ref> Highly public accusations of greenwashing have contributed to the term's increasing use.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Seele |first1=Peter |last2=Gatti |first2=Lucia |date=2015 |title=Greenwashing Revisited: In Search of a Typology and Accusation-Based Definition Incorporating Legitimacy Strategies |journal=Business Strategy and the Environment |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=239–252 |bibcode=2017BSEnv..26..239S |doi=10.1002/bse.1912}}</ref>

Moreover, the act of greenwashing directly undermines "green trust" in consumers, which also harms the credibility and profitability of the company making the practice. Accurate [[green marketing]] can serve as a competitive advantage, but its misuse as greenwashing can lead to the company being perceived as morally irresponsible, damaging its reputation.

Greenwashing has recently increased to meet consumer demand for environmentally-friendly goods and services. New regulations, laws, and guidelines put forward by organizations such as the [[Committee of Advertising Practice]] in the UK aim to discourage companies from using greenwashing to deceive consumers.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thornton |first=Gabriella |date=18 May 2022 |title=New Environmental Claims Guidance from CAP, BCAP and the European Commission |url=https://marketinglaw.osborneclarke.com/advertising-regulation/new-environmental-claims-guidance-from-cap-bcap-and-the-european-commission/ |access-date=5 November 2022 |website=marketinglaw.osborneclarke.com |language=en-GB}}</ref> At the same time, activists have been increasingly inclined to accuse companies of greenwashing, with inconsistent standards as to what activities merit such an accusation.<ref name="Harvard" />

==Characteristics==
Activities deemed to be characteristic of greenwashing can vary by time and place, product, and the opinions or expectations of the person making the determination.<ref name="Harvard2">{{cite web |last1=Pears |first1=Peter |last2=Baines |first2=Tim |last3=Williams |first3=Oliver |date=July 24, 2023 |title=Greenwashing: Navigating the Risk |url=https://corpgov.law.harvard.edu/2023/07/24/greenwashing-navigating-the-risk/ |publisher=Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance}}</ref>

According to the [[United Nations]], greenwashing can present itself in many ways, such as claiming that the company will achieve future environment milestones while not putting sufficient plans in place to do so, being intentionally vague about operations or using vague claims that cannot be specifically proven (like saying they are "environmentally friendly" or "green"), saying that a product does not contain harmful materials or use harmful practices that they would not use anyways, highlighting one thing the company does well regarding the environment while not doing anything else, and promoting products that meet regulatory minimums as if peer products do not.<ref name=":42">{{Cite web |author=United Nations |title=Greenwashing – the deceptive tactics behind environmental claims |url=https://www.un.org/en/climatechange/science/climate-issues/greenwashing |access-date=2024-11-18 |website=United Nations |language=en}}</ref>

Additionally, TerraChoice, an environmental consulting division of [[UL (safety organization)|UL]], described the "seven sins of greenwashing" in 2007 to "help consumers identify products that made misleading environmental claims":<ref>{{cite web |title=Sins of Greenwashing |url=https://www.ul.com/insights/sins-greenwashing |access-date=15 November 2022 |publisher=UL Solutions}}</ref>

* "Hidden Trade-off", which claims a product is "green" based on an unreasonably narrow set of attributes without attention to other critical environmental issues.
* "No proof", a claim that cannot be substantiated by easily accessible information or a reliable third-party certification.
* "Vagueness" is a poorly defined or broad claim that the consumer will likely misunderstand, such as 'all-natural.'
* "Worshipping False Labels", which is a claim that, through words or images, gives the impression of a third-party endorsement where none exists.
* "Irrelevance", which is a claim that may be truthful but unimportant or unhelpful to consumers seeking environmentally preferable products. 
* "Lesser of Two Evils", a claim that may be true within the product category, but risks distracting consumers from the more significant environmental impact of the category.
* "Fibbing", which is a claim that is simply false.

Considering these ways of identifying greenwashing, TerraChoice noted that by 2010, approximately 95% of consumer products in the U.S. claiming to be green were discovered to commit at least one of these sins.<ref name=":04">{{cite web |date=2013 |title=The Sins of Greenwashing |url=http://sinsofgreenwashing.org/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140717143618/http://sinsofgreenwashing.org/ |archive-date=17 July 2014 |access-date=30 July 2022 |website=sinsofgreenwashing.org}}</ref><ref name=":12">{{cite news |last1=Gelles |first1=Jeff |date=26 October 2010 |title=Study: 'Greenwashing' mars 95% of 'green' items |url=https://www.inquirer.com/philly/blogs/consumer/Cleaning_up_the_greenwashing.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221115171247/https://www.inquirer.com/philly/blogs/consumer/Cleaning_up_the_greenwashing.html |archive-date=November 15, 2022 |access-date=15 November 2022 |newspaper=The Philadelphia Inquirer}}</ref>

The characteristics and concept of greenwashing are vaguely defined, and some only consider environmental claims, while others also factor in deception regarding corporate social responsibility (CSR). Additionally, scholars make a distinction between an object's attributes view, which focuses on whether a product's environmental claims align with its features, and the process attribute view, which examines whether the firm's environmental efforts match its promotional efforts.<ref name="ReferenceA"/>

== Types of greenwashing ==
Greenwashing can take different forms, which change depending on where and how the environmental misconduct or environmental claim occurs within an organization or its supply chain. These types change how stakeholders blame, judge, and decide whether to support or even invest in a firm.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nemes |first1=Noémi |last2=Scanlan |first2=Stephen J. |last3=Smith |first3=Pete |last4=Smith |first4=Tone |last5=Aronczyk |first5=Melissa |last6=Hill |first6=Stephanie |last7=Lewis |first7=Simon L. |last8=Montgomery |first8=A. Wren |last9=Tubiello |first9=Francesco N. |last10=Stabinsky |first10=Doreen |date=2022-04-08 |title=An Integrated Framework to Assess Greenwashing |journal=Sustainability |language=en |volume=14 |issue=8 |pages=4431 |doi=10.3390/su14084431 |bibcode=2022Sust...14.4431N |doi-access=free |issn=2071-1050}}</ref>

The first type is direct greenwashing, which occurs when a firm's own processes are inconsistent with its environmental claims and lead to blaming the entire company and having low intention to invest.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cartellier |first1=Fanny |last2=Tankov |first2=Peter |last3=Zerbib |first3=Olivier David |date=2025-11-01 |title=Can investors curb greenwashing? |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165188925001617 |journal=Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control |volume=180 |article-number=105195 |doi=10.1016/j.jedc.2025.105195 |issn=0165-1889}}</ref>

The second type is indirect greenwashing, which happens when a supplier makes false environmental claims, thus the company it supplies is also negatively impacted and is blamed even though the company itself did not commit any misconduct.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Yue |last2=Jung |first2=Sojin |date=2025-10-23 |title=The aftermath of greenwashing in the fashion industry: Chinese consumer responses to different types of greenwashing |url=https://www.emerald.com/apjml/article/37/9/2669/1248632/The-aftermath-of-greenwashing-in-the-fashion |journal=Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics |language=en |volume=37 |issue=9 |pages=2669–2685 |doi=10.1108/APJML-06-2024-0858 |issn=1355-5855|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Badhwar |first1=Aayushi |last2=Islam |first2=Saniyat |last3=Tan |first3=Caroline Swee Lin |last4=Panwar |first4=Tarun |last5=Wigley |first5=Stephen |last6=Nayak |first6=Rajkishore |date=2024-03-26 |title=Unraveling Green Marketing and Greenwashing: A Systematic Review in the Context of the Fashion and Textiles Industry |journal=Sustainability |language=en |volume=16 |issue=7 |pages=2738 |doi=10.3390/su16072738 |bibcode=2024Sust...16.2738B |doi-access=free |issn=2071-1050}}</ref>

The third type is vicarious greenwashing, which occurs when a “green” company partners with a non-environmentally friendly supplier. In this case the company is held liable for the supplier's misconduct because of its stated commitment to sustainability.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-07-26 |title=How to spot and avoid greenwashing in supply chains |url=https://www.businessthink.unsw.edu.au/articles/greenwashing-supply-chains |access-date=2025-12-11 |website=www.businessthink.unsw.edu.au |language=en}}</ref>

Additionally, some scholars argue that the more internal and intentional the greenwashing, the more blame and less investment the company receives.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pizzetti |first1=Marta |last2=Gatti |first2=Lucia |last3=Seele |first3=Peter |date=2021-04-01 |title=Firms Talk, Suppliers Walk: Analyzing the Locus of Greenwashing in the Blame Game and Introducing 'Vicarious Greenwashing' |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10551-019-04406-2 |journal=Journal of Business Ethics |language=en |volume=170 |issue=1 |pages=21–38 |doi=10.1007/s10551-019-04406-2 |issn=1573-0697|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Greenwashing can also take different forms depending on whether it is on a firm-level or a product-level.

“Product-level greenwashing” mainly focuses on the products or services provided by the company. On this level, “claim greenwashing” occurs when there is a use of misleading statements about the environmental benefits and vague, unverified, and false certifications such as “eco-friendly”. Moreover, "executional greenwashing” happens when companies rely on visuals and symbols, such as green colors and nature imagery, that connect to sustainability and mislead consumers into believing that a product is more ecological than it is. These tactics, which are also known as the “sins of greenwashing”, tend to hide the negative impacts and diminish the consumer trust.<ref name=":32">{{Cite journal |last1=de Freitas Netto |first1=Sebastião Vieira |last2=Sobral |first2=Marcos Felipe Falcão |last3=Ribeiro |first3=Ana Regina Bezerra |last4=Soares |first4=Gleibson Robert da Luz |date=2020-02-11 |title=Concepts and forms of greenwashing: a systematic review |journal=Environmental Sciences Europe |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=19 |doi=10.1186/s12302-020-0300-3 |doi-access=free |issn=2190-4715}}</ref>

On the other hand, “firm-level greenwashing” happens at the organizational level, for example when a firm uses advertising and campaigns to promote sustainability while still having operations that damage the environment. This misleads the reputation and image of corporate responsibility, which confuses consumers through both words and imagery, leading to marketing deception on authentic environmental efforts.<ref name=":32" />

More generally, and in the physical world, the term "beauty strip" is used pejoratively to describe the practice of hiding unsightly logging, mining and other extractive land uses with a "beauty strip"<ref>{{Cite web|title=How Green are Oregon's Forest Management Practices?|url=https://www.earthisland.org/journal/index.php/articles/entry/how_green_are_oregons_forest_management_practices/|website=Earth Island Journal|access-date=2025-11-30|quote=The film's footage is stark and dramatic, taking viewers, "behind locked gates" and "beyond the beauty strip" – the curtain of tall trees left along roadsides to mask the clearcuts that lie beyond. Shot after shot shows acres of denuded hillsides dotted with stumps.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Beware the greenwash|url=https://www.connectsavannah.com/community-2/beware-the-greenwash-2536432/|website=Connect Savannah|date=2015-03-11|access-date=2025-11-30|language=en-US|first=Jessica Leigh|last=Lebos}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=BEYOND THE BEAUTY STRIP: Saving What's Left of Our Forests|publisher=Camden House|date=|first=Mitch|last=Lansky |ol=9825246M }}</ref> of trees or other tall vegetation, perhaps even required by government to maintain community aesthetics.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=The perceived scenic effects of clearcutting in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, USA|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S030147970700237X|journal=Journal of Environmental Management|date=2008-11-01|issn=0301-4797|pages=167–183|volume=89|series=Our Shared Landscape: Design, Planning and Management of Multifunctional Landscapes|issue=3|doi=10.1016/j.jenvman.2007.01.064|first=James F.|last=Palmer |pmid=17825474 |bibcode=2008JEnvM..89..167P |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==History==

The origins of greenwashing can be traced to several different moments. For example, [[Keep America Beautiful]] was a campaign founded by beverage manufacturers and others in 1953.<ref>{{cite web |title=Business-Managed Environment – Front Groups – Keep America Beautiful |url= https://www.herinst.org/BusinessManagedDemocracy/environment/fronts/KAB.html |website=herinst.org |date=2017 |access-date=15 November 2022}}</ref> The campaign focused on recycling and littering, diverting attention away from corporate responsibility to protect the environment. The objective was to forestall the regulation of disposable containers, such as the one established by [[Vermont]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Abdelfatah |first1=Rund |title=The Litter Myth: Throughline |url= https://www.npr.org/transcripts/757539617 |website=NPR.org |date=5 September 2019 |access-date=15 November 2022}}</ref>

In the mid-1960s, the environmental movement gained momentum, particularly after the publication of the landmark [[Silent Spring]] by [[Rachel Carson]]. The book marked a turning point in environmental awareness and inspired citizen action. It prompted many companies to seek a new, cleaner or greener image through advertising, although others, like [[E. Bruce Harrison]], known as the father of modern greenwashing, sought to defame Carson and disparage the message of her book.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://drilled.media/news/harrison-1 |title=E. Bruce Harrison: The godfather of greenwashing |website= www.drilled.media| publisher= Drilled|date= 6 July 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.thenation.com/article/environment/climate-change-compromise/|title=There can be no compromise on a burning planet |website= www.thenation.com| publisher= The Nation|date= 27 October 2021}}</ref> [[Jerry Mander]], a former [[Madison Avenue]] advertising executive, called this new form of advertising "ecopornography."<ref>{{cite book |last=Black |first=Brian |url= https://archive.org/details/greatdebatesamer00blac |title=Great Debates in American Environmental History |publisher=Greenwood Press |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-313-33930-1 |editor-last=Lybecker |editor-first=Donna L. |location=Westport |page= [https://archive.org/details/greatdebatesamer00blac/page/n171 147] |url-access=limited}}</ref>

[[File:Earth Day - Enact 1970.jpg|thumb|Earth Day 1970|273x273px]]

The first [[Earth Day]] was held on 22 April 1970. Most companies did not actively participate in the initial Earth Day events because environmental issues were not a major corporate priority, and there was a sense of skepticism or resistance to the movement's message. Nevertheless, some industries began to advertise themselves as environmentally friendly. For example, public utilities were estimated to have spent around $300 million advertising themselves as clean and green companies, which was eight times what they spent on pollution reduction research.<ref name="tglo2">{{cite web |date=6 July 2012 |title=Greenwashing 101 |url= http://thegreenlifeonline.org/greenwash101/ |access-date=7 July 2016 |website=thegreenlifeonline.org}}</ref><ref name="gfs2">{{cite web |date=22 March 2001 |title=Greenwash Fact Sheet |url= http://www.corpwatch.org/article.php?id=242 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170207224534/http://www.corpwatch.org/article.php?id=242 |archive-date=7 February 2017 |access-date=7 July 2016 |website=corpwatch.org}}</ref>

The term "greenwashing" was coined by New York [[environmentalist]] [[Jay Westerveld]] in a 1986 essay about the [[Hospitality industry|hotel industry's]] hypocritical practice of placing notices in bedrooms promoting the reuse of towels to "save the environment". He noted that these institutions often made little or no effort toward reducing energy waste, although towel reuse saved them laundry costs. He concluded that the fundamental objective was most frequently increased profit. He labeled this and other profitable-but-ineffective "environmentally-conscientious" acts as "greenwashing", introducing properly the term as the act of a company appearing more environmentally friendly than it actually is, often through selective disclosure, misleading advertising, or exaggerated claims.<ref>{{cite web |last=Motavalli |first=Jim |date=12 February 2011 |title=A History of Greenwashing: How Dirty Towels Impacted the Green Movement |url=https://www.aol.com/2011/02/12/the-history-of-greenwashing-how-dirty-towels-impacted-the-green/ |access-date=24 December 2023 |work=AOL}}

* {{cite web |last=Hayward |first=Philip |date=1 February 2009 |title=The Real Deal? Hotels grapple with green washing |url=http://www.lodgingmagazine.com/ME2/dirmod.asp?sid=&nm=&type=Publishing&mod=Publications%3A%3AArticle&mid=8F3A7027421841978F18BE895F87F791&tier=4&id=FD212DB2AA944808BF5CE6519B2BCC06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090205171221/http://www.lodgingmagazine.com/ME2/dirmod.asp?sid=&nm=&type=Publishing&mod=Publications%3A%3AArticle&mid=8F3A7027421841978F18BE895F87F791&tier=4&id=FD212DB2AA944808BF5CE6519B2BCC06 |archive-date=5 February 2009 |work=Lodging Magazine online}}

* {{cite news |last1=Romero |first1=Purple |date=17 September 2008 |title=Beware of green marketing, warns Greenpeace exec |url=https://www.abs-cbn.com/special-report/09/16/08/beware-green-marketing-warns-greenpeace-exec |access-date=24 December 2023 |website=news.abs-cbn.com}}</ref>

In 1991, a study published in the "Journal of Public Policy and Marketing" ([[American Marketing Association]]) found that 58% of environmental ads had at least one deceptive claim. Another study found that 77% of people said a company's environmental reputation affected whether they would buy its products. One-fourth of all household products marketed around Earth Day advertised themselves as being green and environmentally friendly. In 1998, the [[Federal Trade Commission]] created the "Green Guidelines", which defined terms used in environmental marketing. The following year, the FTC ruled that the Nuclear Energy Institute's claims of environmental cleanliness were invalid. However, the FTC took no action regarding the ads because they fell outside the agency's jurisdiction. This caused the FTC to realize they needed new, clear, enforceable standards. In 1999, the word "greenwashing" was added to the "[[Oxford English Dictionary]]."<ref name="tglo2"/><ref name="gfs2"/>

Days before the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, Greenpeace released ''The Greenpeace Book on Greenwash'', which described the corporate takeover of the UN conference and provided case studies of the contrast between corporate polluters and their rhetoric. Third World Network published an expanded version of that report, "Greenwash: The Reality Behind Corporate Environmentalism", in 1996.<ref>Greer, J., [https://archive.org/details/greenwashreality0000gree/page/n263/mode/2up Greenwash : the reality behind corporate environmentalism], ''Third World Network'': Penang, Malaysia</ref>

In 2002, during the [[World Summit on Sustainable Development]] in Johannesburg, the Greenwashing Academy hosted the Greenwash Academy Awards. The ceremony awarded companies like [[BP]], [[ExxonMobil]], and even the [[Federal government of the United States|U.S. Government]] for their elaborate greenwashing ads and support for greenwashing.<ref name="tglo2"/><ref name="gfs2"/> A 2020 European Union study found that over 50% of examined environmental claims in the EU were vague, misleading, or unfounded, while 40% of them were unsubstantiated.<ref>{{cite web |title=Consumer protection: enabling sustainable choices and ending greenwashing |url=https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_23_1692 |access-date=2024-06-26 |work=European Commission – European Commission}}</ref>

Many companies have committed to reducing their greenhouse gas emissions to net zero after the [[Paris Agreement]] was signed in 2015. A net zero emissions level means that any emissions given off by a company would be offset by carbon sequestrators in the natural world (also known as carbon sinks). However, companies are not actually cutting emissions, but are creating unfeasible plans and attempting to improve other things rather than their emissions. Therefore, most companies are not actually upholding their agreements and ultimately continue not to cause any positive change.<ref name=":42"/>

=== Social media and influencers ===
{{AI-generated|section=Social media|date=January 2026|reason=[[Special:Diff/1326229388|This 2025 edit]], note [[WP:AISIGNS]] (section summary, vocab distribution typical of 2025 LLMs, etc}}
The role of social media in everyday life and the rise of social media platforms have transformed how organisations communicate about their environmental claims. This leads to new forms of greenwashing in the digital age.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Zhang |first=Jie |date=2025-05-08 |title=The Role of Social Media in Promoting Environmental Sustainability |url=https://www.sdgsreview.org/LifestyleJournal/article/view/6586 |journal=Journal of Lifestyle and SDGS Review |volume=5 |issue=5 |article-number=e06586 |doi=10.47172/2965-730X.SDGsReview.v5.n05.pe06586 |issn=2965-730X|doi-access=free }}</ref> Social media allows companies to reach a large audience through visually appealing content. This content can sometimes promote products or ways of living as environmentally friendly. Scholars have previously noted that this creates a highly persuasive context in which sustainability claims may be exaggerated or misrepresented.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tazeen |first1=Farah |last2=Mullick |first2=N.H. |date=2023-01-07 |title=The Impact of Social Media Platforms 'Facebook and Instagram' in Influencing Purchasing Behaviour of Green Products |url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/09722629221133960 |journal=Vision: The Journal of Business Perspective |article-number=09722629221133960 |language=en |doi=10.1177/09722629221133960 |issn=0972-2629|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

A characteristic of greenwashing on social media that is becoming more popular is the role of influencers. Influencers are often perceived as trustworthy sources due to the parasocial relationships they have with their audiences.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Breves |first1=Priska |last2=Liebers |first2=Nicole |date=2022-08-18 |title=#Greenfluencing. The Impact of Parasocial Relationships with Social Media Influencers on Advertising Effectiveness and Followers' Pro-environmental Intentions |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17524032.2022.2109708 |journal=Environmental Communication |language=en |volume=16 |issue=6 |pages=773–787 |doi=10.1080/17524032.2022.2109708 |bibcode=2022Ecomm..16..773B |issn=1752-4032}}</ref> Followers can interpret claims made by influencers saying a product is eco-friendly or sustainable as credible, even if the actual environmental benefits are minimal.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Vilkaite-Vaitone |first=Neringa |date=2024-02-07 |title=From Likes to Sustainability: How Social Media Influencers Are Changing the Way We Consume |journal=Sustainability |language=en |volume=16 |issue=4 |page=1393 |doi=10.3390/su16041393 |bibcode=2024Sust...16.1393V |doi-access=free |issn=2071-1050}}</ref> Scholars have proved that the dynamic between influencers and their audience can increase, particularly younger audiences' sensitivity to misleading messaging regarding environmental claims, since often the trust these consumers have in the influencers is higher than the trust in the company producing the product.<ref name=":5" />

Companies and influencers play a large role in how their environmental claims are perceived on social media. Their posts can include nature imagery, such as forests or green colour palettes, to help create an aesthetic association with being environmentally friendly.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=OECD |date=2025-05-11 |title=Protecting and empowering consumers in the green transition: Misleading green claims |url=https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/protecting-and-empowering-consumers-in-the-green-transition_12f28e4f-en.html |journal=OECD Digital Economy Papers |language=en |doi=10.1787/12f28e4f-en|url-access=subscription }}</ref> These visuals in a post can almost overpower the lack of factual environmental. Research shows that greenwashing where imagery substitutes evidence, also called symbolic greenwashing, is particularly seen in industries such as fashion and cosmetics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fella |first1=Stefanie |last2=Bausa |first2=Elena |date=2024-05-01 |title=Green or greenwashed? Examining consumers' ability to identify greenwashing |journal=Journal of Environmental Psychology |volume=95 |article-number=102281 |doi=10.1016/j.jenvp.2024.102281 |issn=0272-4944|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Muzhen |last2=Cavender |first2=RayeCarol |last3=Lee |first3=Min-Young |date=2025-03-27 |title=Consumer Awareness of Fashion Greenwashing: Insights from Social Media Discussions |journal=Sustainability |language=en |volume=17 |issue=7 |page=2982 |doi=10.3390/su17072982 |bibcode=2025Sust...17.2982L |doi-access=free |issn=2071-1050}}</ref>

Another popular trend is the continued use of unregulated terminology such as ''clean, natural'' and ''eco-friendly.'' All these terms are often seen in digital marketing campaigns, although they lack scientific definitions. On social media platforms, these terms can be repeated and used through viral trends or sponsored content, which further pushes them to a wider audience.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nabivi |first=Elnur |date=2025-02-25 |title=The Role of Social Media in Green Marketing: How Eco-Friendly Content Influences Brand Attitude and Consumer Engagement |journal=Sustainability |language=en |volume=17 |issue=5 |page=1965 |doi=10.3390/su17051965 |bibcode=2025Sust...17.1965N |doi-access=free |issn=2071-1050}}</ref>

Furthermore, the speed at which social media moves means that misleading content can circulate widely before any fact-checking or regulatory bodies get involved. This rapid spread means that exaggerated sustainability claims can be normalised, which makes them seem more legitimate through repetition alone.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Aïmeur |first1=Esma |last2=Amri |first2=Sabrine |last3=Brassard |first3=Gilles |date=2023-02-09 |title=Fake news, disinformation and misinformation in social media: a review |journal=Social Network Analysis and Mining |language=en |volume=13 |issue=1 |article-number=30 |doi=10.1007/s13278-023-01028-5 |issn=1869-5469 |pmc=9910783 |pmid=36789378}}</ref>

Regulatory bodies in several countries, especially in the EU, have begun addressing greenwashing both on paper and in digital environments. Guidelines issued by authorities such as the European Union emphasise that sustainability claims made online must be clearly defined even in short-form content.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-12-03 |title=Green claims - Environment - European Commission |url=https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/circular-economy-topics/green-claims_en |access-date=2025-12-07 |website=environment.ec.europa.eu |language=en}}</ref>
